overview.explanation: Dashed arrows show borrowed access, not transfer of ownership. Solid arrows show completion dependencies before the final read. The tasks may overlap in time; the diagram does not promise which runs first.

focus.title: Share access without sharing write locations
explain: array stores six integers in each value. input gets 1 through 6; squared{} initializes its six integers to zero.
The lambda captures surrounding variables by reference with [&]. begin and end are value parameters naming a half-open slice.
The loop writes squared[i] from input[i]. Different tasks receive nonoverlapping index ranges.
The brace and semicolon finish the lambda object definition.
focus.what: Both tasks use the same arrays but write different integer objects within squared.
focus.where: The arrays live in main, outside the asynchronous tasks.
focus.why: Independent slices let the work run concurrently without a mutex for these separate elements.
focus.invariant: The arrays must outlive all task access, indices must be in range, and no two tasks may write the same element.
focus.risk: Overlapping slices introduce a data race. Capturing references to destroyed local arrays would access invalid storage.

focus.title: Establish completion before observation
explain: std::launch::async requires asynchronous execution. The first future represents the task for [0,3).
The second task handles [3,6), so every index is assigned exactly once.
get waits for each task’s result and rethrows a task exception if one occurred. Only after both calls does main read the output array.
focus.what: A future is a handle through which the caller waits for a task’s result or exception.
focus.where: These lines sit between constructing the lambda and printing/reducing squared.
focus.why: Completion synchronization makes the finished writes visible before the later reads.
focus.invariant: The reduction begins after both get calls. The squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 and their sum is 91.
focus.risk: Reading squared before completion can race with task writes. This CPU example neither launches a CUDA kernel nor proves a speedup.
